newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten says HK's future leader democrat at heart.
newsitem.headline: Patten says HK's future leader democrat at heart.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten said on Saturday his post-colonial successor, Tung Chee-hwa, was a democrat at heart.
"I think he is a more, with a small c, conservative man than I am," Patten said in a BBC interview.
"He, I think, always believes that the process of democratisation should be...a more stately pace than I think is appropriate. I am sure in his heart he is a democrat," he said.

Tung, a former shipping tycoon, will take over the helm from Patten at midnight on June 30 when the British colony returns to Chinese rule. He was chosen on December 11 by a 400-strong Selection Committee assembled under China's close supervision.

Patten, who antagonised China when he introduced electoral reforms in Hong Kong in 1992, said he believed Tung would head towards one-person one-vote in the future, but it would be at a much slower pace.
"I think he would probably believe we should arrive at that destination at a rather slower pace than I think desirable," he said.

Hong Kong people will likely be given a chance to vote in 1998's Legislative Council election, the first under Chinese rule. But the number of seats to be directly or indirectly elected is expected to be limited.
The current chamber set up under Patten's reforms, which has 20 directly elected seats and the rest returned by indirect vote, has run foul of Beijing.
China has said Patten's reforms violated a Sino-British agreement which stipulates democratisation in Hong Kong should be enlarged gradually.
Beijing will install a provisional body, which was chosen by the Selection Committee on December 21, to replace the elected legislature upon the handover.
Tung was in the Chinese capital on Saturday to hold his first set of working-level talks with Chinese officials.
